title: Vedanta (revisited)
hook: how do you start a new school of thought without a new scripture? in Vedanta, you write on the books everyone already shares

segments.voice: Yesterday Vedanta heard one line, you are that, three ways: not-two, body and soul, two who stay close. Did you let someone read something their way? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

Say you have a new insight about the deepest things. You're sure of it. How do you get anyone to take it seriously? You could announce a new book. You could gather followers. In Vedanta, the answer is quieter and much harder. You sit down with the books everybody already reads, the ones your rivals read too, and you go through them line by line, showing how your insight was there all along. Yesterday's three teachers didn't each bring their own scripture. They brought commentaries on the same shelf. Today: what's on that shelf, and why a whole school of thought agrees to argue there.
screen: `A NEW INSIGHT.` → `NO NEW BOOK.` → `WRITE ON THE SHARED SHELF.`

segments.voice: Tradition names the shelf the prasthanas, the starting points, and it names them together. The Upanishads, the teachings at the end of the Veda, which tradition counts as shruti, what was heard. The Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna on the battlefield, part of the Mahabharata, a text of smriti, what was remembered. And the Brahma Sutra, the short, packed lines that try to gather what the Upanishads teach and answer objections. Tradition describes them as a starting point in revelation, one in remembered teaching, and one in reasoning. Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva each wrote a commentary on the Brahma Sutra and on the Gita, and each read the Upanishads closely. That's how a Vedanta school stands up: by showing that its reading makes sense of the shared texts, all of them, including the hard verses. The Brahma Sutra itself says why this matters. Early on, it says, in effect, that Brahman is known from the Upanishads because they all fit together around it. The texts aren't a pile. They're meant to agree. So every teacher's task is to show the agreement, and the arguments between the schools are arguments about how the pieces fit. There's something generous in that. Nobody gets to win by changing the subject. You stay with the same pages your neighbor reads, and you keep reading until you can say, here, this is what I see.
screen: `THE STARTING POINTS.` · `HEARD, REMEMBERED, REASONED.` · `EVERY SCHOOL WRITES ON THE SAME SHELF.` · `THE TEXTS ARE MEANT TO AGREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with something you already have. Settle, and let one line you know come to mind. It can be from any text you love, a verse, a song, a thing someone wise once told you. Say it inwardly, slowly. Then ask: what's here that I haven't seen before? Don't hunt for a clever answer. Let the line sit, the way the Vedanta teachers sat with their shared pages, and see what it shows you when you stay. If you pray, you can hold that line as an offering. The bell holds the time.
Vedanta. Today, its shared shelf: the Upanishads, the Gita, the Brahma Sutra, and every school showing how they fit. Today's word.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. Today, before offering a new idea in a conversation, show where it was already there in what the other person said. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: In Vedanta lineages, a teacher's standing rests on commentary: students read the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutra through their own school's commentaries, and the founders of the major schools each commented on the Brahma Sutra and the Gita.

trapdoor: what you thought: each school of Hindu thought has its own holy book.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 1.1.4 (Brahman is known from the Upanishads, because they agree in it)
Bhagavad Gita (Krishna's teaching to Arjuna, within the Mahabharata)
commentaries of Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva on the Brahma Sutra and the Bhagavad Gita

notes: The term prasthana-traya means 'three starting points'; the script avoids stating the count and the etymology. Confirm the framing of shruti, smriti and nyaya prasthanas.

Ramanuja wrote the Shri Bhashya and a Gita Bhashya, but no separate commentaries on individual Upanishads (his Vedartha Sangraha treats them); the script says only that each 'read the Upanishads closely'. Confirm.
Brahma Sutra 1.1.4 (tat tu samanvayat) paraphrased as the Upanishads agreeing in Brahman; confirm.
Classifying the Gita as smriti is standard but some traditions treat it with near-shruti status; a Keeper may want that noted.
Editor: 'which Hindus count as shruti' became 'which tradition counts as shruti' (no claim about all Hindus); the carry is spoken as 'Vedanta, revisited'.
